extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, short-form performers and workshop leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for selecting, running and adjudicating short-form improv games in workshops and shows, including how to enforce rules, when to use certain games, and how to get best effects from specific games (e.g., Questions Only, New Choice, Half Life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty options for infractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible consequences when an improviser breaks a rule: they must take the sentence back and try again; another improviser takes over; they lose a 'life'; the scene ends and they have lost; they endure a token punishment, such as having wet sponges thrown at them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different penalties have different effects. Some are helpful but some (e.g., wet sponges) can be very destructive. Choose punishments that preserve the seriousness and authority of judges/hosts; avoid penalties that reduce the work to a kids' show or destroy performers' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience role in enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the audience should spot infractions or whether the host/director/judge will do so (e.g., in No S the audience hisses at infractions; in Alphabet audience abuse is asked to begin with the omitted letter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what you want the audience to contribute and whether audience policing will produce the desired effects. Use audience participation where it enhances fun without undermining judges or show seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match enforcement to game difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose enforcement procedures appropriate to how difficult the game is for performers (e.g., for Three Word Sentences host calls errors and line is re-taken; for Scenes in Rhyme provide substitution lifeline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harder restrictions benefit from permissive lifelines or backstage support; easier restrictions can be strictly policed. Tailor error-calling and remediation to preserve performance flow and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'complexed-up' distortions that destroy the game's core
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding hoops or mechanical complications (e.g., X Word Sentences where every performer must speak N words, or a caller changing the number) can swamp the action and make the game look the same every time, distracting from story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't add gimmicks that shift attention from story to the game mechanic. Keep focus on behaviors the game is intended to train (brevity, offers, relationship) rather than on arbitrary difficulty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions Only: basic technical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every utterance must be one sentence and that sentence must be a legitimate question. Do not allow non-questions or conversational fragments that are effectively statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist non-questions are struck out and retaken (other improvisers can police this). Consider playing in pairs first and replacing anyone who hesitates or utters a statement when performing for an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions Only: performance strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: To make Questions Only advance, add information and assumptions, mentally answer questions 'yes' and then ask next obvious question, make physical offers, and add emotional reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'yes-and' thinking to create a platform and move the scene forward; mime physical offers without degenerating into full mime; deliberately add emotional reactions to create change and story despite the restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Questions Only to spot waffle vs story offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions Only sharpens awareness of 'waffle' (aimless conversational circling) versus 'story offers' (offers that move narrative forward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Questions Only as an exercise to learn to make strong offers—play it short and value the difficulty rather than expecting long narrative payoff in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons to play a particular game (selection criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible reasons: to strengthen a particular muscle in workshops; because the challenge adds an extra layer of interest; because the procedure is inherently amusing; because it provides a framework to demonstrate wit/skill; because it inspires different offers; because it enforces desirable behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these reasons as criteria when selecting games—pick games for the specific training or audience effect you want rather than at random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match game to players and moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Select games that suit particular performers and performing situations; use games to put improvisers and audiences in particular states and to contrast with preceding pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider performers' strengths (storytellers vs gag merchants), audience expectations, and the show's pacing. For example, follow a hysterical clown game with a dramatic Three Word Sentence to create contrast; after an epic, play a quick high-energy game like Half Life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'Good Games'
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Games enforce otherwise desirable behavior, train particular improvisation 'muscles', and often involve storytelling—making them useful both in workshops and onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor games that build habits you want to encourage (brevity, offers, narrative) and that transfer to open scenes rather than only being clever mechanical tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'Dumb But Fun' games
rubrics_metrics.description: Games that are entertaining or amusing and may have utility but can teach bad habits or are pointlessly novel (e.g., some repeat or gag-driven games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are acceptable occasionally for variety or morale, but be aware they can encourage habits counterproductive to narrative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'Never Play' games
rubrics_metrics.description: Games that are pointlessly stupid or consistently harmful to storytelling (e.g., First Line/Last Line which often produces a joyless plod or a contrived, forced ending).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid games whose mechanics make it nearly impossible to produce satisfying story outcomes, or use them only for deliberate training with clear expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Choice: how to play
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players plus a caller; when the caller announces 'new choice' the last player to speak must replace their last line with something new; lines edited out make no further impact on the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate rather than over-describe; keep the game short; the caller should intercede frequently enough to maintain pressure and risk without breaking the scene entirely.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Choice: playing the game well (technical demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Players must avoid babbling, speaking in paragraphs, or talking over each other so the caller can clearly intercede; leave a half-second of space after utterances; make arbitrary choices to allow calling; callers should sense when to push.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage improvisers to blurt without overthinking; callers should 'new choice' more when performers are playing safe; keep it energetic and short; good callers preserve audience excitement by not sparing players when the scene is 'going well.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New Choice: what it's good for
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent workshop exercise to loosen players and reassure them of creative abundance; in shows, a high-energy opener or lift that exposes improvisational risk and effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not appropriate for longform, thoughtful pieces (e.g., Harold-like work), but ideal as short-form opener or crowd-pleaser; bears repeated viewings if kept tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Choice: variants and spin-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants include ringing a bell instead of saying 'New choice', giving the bell to an audience member, calling it 'Shouldasaid', audience shouting 'new choice' as finale, and spin-offs like 'Perfect Pitch' where an audience member controls accept/reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants can alter audience involvement or the game's flavor—ensure technical demands (pauses, clarity) are maintained and adapt caller/player roles thoughtfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half Life: structure and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene is played in 60 seconds, then repeated in 30, 15, 7, 5, and 2 seconds; the caller calls 'Go!' and 'Time!' at each interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caller must call times crisply (audience member as timer can be risky). Start with a simple 60-second scene with a few big physical offers that serve as 'tent poles' for subsequent compressed versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half Life: how to play well
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial scene should be simple with big physical offers; improvisers should try to pack as much as possible as the scene collapses while being willing to take shortcuts; the caller-player relationship can be used to add theatricality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the game sparingly as a show boost or finale; allow the caller to 'cheat' timings slightly rather than leaving performers hanging; reverse-order variants generally don't work well.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Line/Last Line: pitfalls and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The game gives two lines from the audience and the scene must begin with the first and end with the last. The last line must make perfect sense in light of what preceded and also ideally be surprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common failures: (a) forcing a contrived ending by remembering the last line late, producing square-peg endings, or (b) structuring the scene as a slow plod toward an obvious endpoint. If attempted, either boldly ignore the last line until late with strong storytelling, or build the possibility of the last line early without flattening the scene—both approaches are difficult and risky.
